body: McLean and Pontiff, 'Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?' (Journal of Finance 71(1), 2016; ~920 Semantic Scholar citations) studied 97 published US return predictors. Compared with the original sample period, average long-short returns were about 26% lower in the window after the sample ended but before publication, which is their estimate of statistical bias or data-mining. They were about 58% lower after publication. That implies roughly 32% of the decay comes from investors trading on the published result. The decay was larger for predictors with bigger in-sample returns, and smaller for predictors concentrated in stocks that are costly to arbitrage (small, illiquid, high idiosyncratic risk). After publication, trading volume, variance and short interest in the anomaly stocks rose. Replicated: yes. Similar decay appears in international samples, and Chen-Zimmermann find about a 50% post-publication drop. Use for us: (1) budget about half the published premium for any known anomaly; (2) the most durable residual edges sit where arbitrage is expensive, which is partly Indian small and micro caps, but those also carry the impact and governance costs; (3) the most durable edge is information nobody has published, such as our promise tracker and filing diffs, not another public screen.
title: McLean-Pontiff (JF 2016): anomaly returns fall ~26% out-of-sample and ~58% after publication
